items.title: How to Make a Budget | Beginner's Guide to Budgeting

blocks.md:
A budget is a plan for your money. It tells every dollar where to go before you spend it.

Money comes **in**. That's your income, like an allowance, gifts or pay from a job. Money goes **out**. That's spending, saving and sharing.

A budget is not about saying no to everything. It's about choosing what matters most to you.

**A quick example**
Maya gets $20 a week for chores. Without a plan, it's gone by Tuesday. With a plan, she decides first:
• $10 to spend on fun things
• $6 to save for new headphones
• $4 to give or save for later

Same $20. Now Maya is in charge of it.
**Try this:** For one week, write down every dollar you spend. Most people are surprised where their money goes.

items.title: Needs, wants and your money brain

blocks.md:
**Needs** are things you must have to live, learn or work. Think food, a place to live, basic clothes and getting to school or work.

**Wants** are nice extras. Think games, snacks, concert tickets and the newest phone.

Wants aren't bad. The trick is paying for needs first.

**Why do we overspend?**
• Ads are made to make us want things right now
• Friends buy stuff, and we want to keep up
• Buying something feels good for a moment
• Small buys add up without us noticing

**The 24-hour rule**
Want something that isn't a need? Wait one day before you buy it. If you still want it tomorrow, it may be worth it. Often the feeling fades.
**Parent tip:** Talk out loud when you shop. "We need milk. We want ice cream. Let's check the budget." Kids learn a lot by hearing how you decide.

blocks.md:
The 50/30/20 rule is a simple way to split money you take home.

• **50% for needs:** rent, food, bills, transport
• **30% for wants:** fun, eating out, hobbies
• **20% for savings:** emergency fund, goals and paying down debt

**Example with $2,000 a month**
• Needs: $1,000
• Wants: $600
• Savings: $400

Saving $400 a month adds up to $4,800 in a year.

**A kid-sized version**
If you don't pay rent yet, you can use the same idea. Try 50% to spend, 30% to save for a goal and 20% to save for the long term or give.

It's a starting point, not a law. If rent is high where you live, needs might take more than half. Adjust it so it works for you.

blocks.md:
An emergency fund is money you save just for surprises. A broken phone. A car repair. A lost job.

Without one, people often turn to credit cards. That can turn one bad day into months of debt.

**How much?**
For adults, many experts suggest 3 to 6 months of basic costs. That sounds like a lot, so start small. Even $500 covers many surprises.

For kids, a "surprise fund" of $20 to $50 can replace lost earbuds or a broken charger.

**Where to keep it**
Keep it somewhere safe and easy to reach, but not too easy. A savings account at a bank or credit union is a good choice. Most are insured by the FDIC or NCUA, so your money is protected.

**Only for real emergencies**
A sale is not an emergency. If you use the fund, refill it next.
**Try this:** Pick a number for your surprise fund. Write it on a sticky note and track your progress.

question.prompt: An emergency fund is usually meant to cover…
question.hint: Think surprise job loss or a big car repair.
question.explanation: Most experts suggest 3 to 6 months of essential costs, kept somewhere safe and easy to reach.

blocks.md:
The easiest way to save is to not think about it.

**Pay yourself first**
When money comes in, save first. Then spend what's left. Most people do the opposite and save whatever is left over. Usually, nothing is left.

**Let it happen on its own**
• Set up an automatic transfer to savings on payday
• Use separate savings "buckets" for each goal
• Round up purchases and save the change

**Make your savings grow**
Some savings accounts pay more interest than others. A high-yield savings account can grow your money faster, and it's still insured. Compare the rate, called APY, before you open one.

**Name your goals**
"Save money" is hard to stick with. "Save $150 for a bike by June" is easier. Clear goals keep you going.

Every budget hits bumps. That's normal. Here's how to handle the common ones.

**"My income changes every month."**
Plan with your lowest month. Extra money in good months goes to savings.

**"I forgot to track."**
Pick one easy tool, like an app or a notebook. Check it once a week, not every day.

**"I blew my budget."**
It happens. Don't quit. Look at what happened and adjust next month.

**"It feels too strict."**
Give yourself a small amount of fun money with no rules. It makes the rest easier to follow.

**Check in every month**
Sit down once a month and ask three questions:
1. Did I spend on what matters to me?
2. What surprised me?
3. What will I change next month?
**Parent tip:** A short monthly money meeting with your kids builds the habit. Keep it to 10 minutes and keep it positive.
